```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE,
  comment = "#>"
)
```

`nlp_find_abbreviations()` finds abbreviations that a text defines for itself and pairs each short form with its long form. Parenthetical definitions -- *"tumor necrosis factor (TNF)"* or *"TNF (tumor necrosis factor)"* -- are found with the Schwartz & Hearst (2003) algorithm; taxonomic abbreviations like *"E. coli"* are matched to *"Escherichia coli"* elsewhere in the same document. This vignette runs it over a set of biomedical Wikipedia articles, looks at short forms shared across documents, and then uses the pairs as a dictionary so that a concept is counted whether it is written out or abbreviated.

Load packages.

```{r libs}
library(textpress)
library(dplyr)
library(DT)
```

## Corpus

Fetch Wikipedia articles on inflammation and gut bacteria, then scrape the article bodies.

```{r corpus}
wiki_urls <- c(
  textpress::fetch_wiki_urls("tumor necrosis factor inflammation", limit = 4),
  textpress::fetch_wiki_urls("Escherichia coli gut microbiota", limit = 4)
)

wiki_text_list <- textpress::read_urls(wiki_urls, exclude_wiki_refs = TRUE)
```

`read_urls()` returns one row per text node. Give each article an integer `doc_id`.

```{r docs}
wiki_text <- wiki_text_list$text |>
  mutate(doc_id = match(url, unique(url))) |>
  relocate(doc_id, .before = 1)

wiki_text |> distinct(doc_id, url)
```

## Find abbreviations

`nlp_find_abbreviations()` pools all rows that share the `by` values into one unit, so with `by = "doc_id"` each article is searched whole: a definition in one paragraph pairs with a full name in another. It returns one row per unique `short_form`/`long_form` pair per unit, along with the `method` that found it.

```{r find}
abbrevs <- wiki_text |>
  textpress::nlp_find_abbreviations(by = "doc_id")

abbrevs |>
  DT::datatable(rownames = FALSE, options = list(pageLength = 10))
```

Run one method on its own with `methods`. The taxonomic pairs read as a species list for the corpus.

```{r taxonomic}
wiki_text |>
  textpress::nlp_find_abbreviations(by = "doc_id", methods = "taxonomic") |>
  DT::datatable(rownames = FALSE, options = list(pageLength = 10))
```

## Shared short forms

Short forms defined in more than one article.

```{r shared}
abbrevs |>
  distinct(doc_id, short_form) |>
  count(short_form, name = "n_docs", sort = TRUE) |>
  filter(n_docs > 1) |>
  DT::datatable(rownames = FALSE)
```

The same short form does not always get the same long form. Different authors spell out *SCFAs* as *"short-chain"*, *"short chain"* or *"small chain fatty acids"*, and the algorithm sometimes takes in a few words too many. Listing every short form with more than one long form is a quick way to find both.

```{r variants}
abbrevs |>
  distinct(short_form, long_form) |>
  group_by(short_form) |>
  filter(n_distinct(tolower(long_form)) > 1) |>
  arrange(short_form) |>
  DT::datatable(rownames = FALSE)
```

## Abbreviation-aware search

Once an article defines *TNF*, it rarely writes out *"tumor necrosis factor"* again, so a search for the long form alone undercounts. Stack the parenthetical pairs into a dictionary in which both forms point to one concept. Where an article spells out a short form more than one way, the first long form becomes the concept and the others become variants of it.

```{r dict}
pairs <- abbrevs |>
  filter(method == "parenthetical") |>
  group_by(doc_id, short_form) |>
  mutate(concept = tolower(first(long_form))) |>
  ungroup()

abbrev_dict <- bind_rows(
  pairs |> transmute(doc_id, form = "short_form", variant = short_form,
                     concept),
  pairs |> transmute(doc_id, form = "long_form", variant = long_form,
                     concept)
) |>
  distinct()
```

Split into sentences and run one `search_dict()` pass over every variant. `search_dict()` matches without regard to case, which is right for long forms but not for short forms: *IS* (insertion sequence) would match every *"is"*. Keep short-form hits only where the case matches, and join each hit to the definitions from its own document.

```{r search}
abbrev_ss <- wiki_text |>
  textpress::nlp_split_sentences(by = c("doc_id", "node_id"))

hits <- abbrev_ss |>
  textpress::search_dict(
    by    = c("doc_id", "node_id", "sentence_id"),
    terms = unique(abbrev_dict$variant)
  ) |>
  mutate(doc_id = as.integer(sub("\\..*$", "", id))) |>
  inner_join(abbrev_dict |> mutate(term = tolower(variant)),
             by = c("doc_id", "term"), relationship = "many-to-many") |>
  filter(form == "long_form" | ngram == variant)
```

Mentions per concept, split by how they were written. Across the corpus, short forms account for most of the mentions.

```{r counts}
hits |>
  distinct(id, start, doc_id, concept, form) |>
  group_by(doc_id, concept) |>
  summarise(
    long_form  = sum(form == "long_form"),
    short_form = sum(form == "short_form"),
    total      = n(),
    .groups    = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(total)) |>
  DT::datatable(rownames = FALSE, options = list(pageLength = 10))
```

## Summary

`nlp_find_abbreviations()` turns the definitions a text already contains into a `short_form`/`long_form` table, using only the text itself and no external dictionary. Listing the pairs by short form exposes spelling variants and noisy matches to clean up; stacking them into a dictionary for `search_dict()` lets a concept be counted whether it is written out or abbreviated. For a fixed vocabulary, see the dictionary search vignette.

Schwartz, A. S., & Hearst, M. A. (2003). A simple algorithm for identifying abbreviation definitions in biomedical text. *Pacific Symposium on Biocomputing*, 451-462.
